title: var vs let vs const
concept: var, let, and const each follow different scope rules

steps.title: var a = 1 (Global Declaration)
steps.explanation:
A variable declared with var has function scope.
Since we're at the global level here, it becomes a global variable.
steps.keyInsight: var is function-scoped. It ignores blocks ({}).

steps.title: let b = 2 (Global Declaration)
steps.explanation:
A variable declared with let has block scope.
We're currently in the global block.
steps.keyInsight: let is block-scoped. It's only valid within the nearest enclosing {}.

steps.title: const c = 3 (Global Declaration)
steps.explanation:
const is also block-scoped.
It behaves like let but cannot be reassigned.

steps.title: Enter if Block
steps.explanation:
We enter the if block.
A new block scope is created.
steps.keyInsight: Every {} creates a new block scope.

steps.title: var a = 10 (The Limit of Function Scope)
steps.explanation:
var treats blocks ({}) as invisible.
It registers the variable in the nearest **function scope** or **global scope** that wraps it.

**Analogy**: Imagine smoking (var) inside a hotel room (block) — the smoke seeps through the walls all the way into the hotel lobby (global scope).
steps.keyInsight: var ignores block boundaries and climbs upward (related to Hoisting).
steps.analogy: Imagine smoking (var) inside a hotel room (block) — the smoke seeps through the walls all the way into the hotel lobby (global scope).

steps.title: let b = 20 (Inside the Block)
steps.explanation:
let is block-scoped.
A new b is created inside the if block.
This is a completely different variable from the global b!
steps.keyInsight: The let b inside the block and the let b in global scope are entirely different variables.

steps.title: const c = 30 (Inside the Block)
steps.explanation:
const is also block-scoped.
A new c is created inside the if block.

steps.title: console.log Inside the Block
steps.explanation:
Print a, b, c from inside the block.
a comes from the global scope (10), while b and c come from the block scope (20, 30).
steps.keyInsight: JavaScript looks for a variable in the nearest scope first.

steps.title: console.log After the Block Ends
steps.explanation:
When the block ends, the block-scoped variables (let b, const c) are gone.
Only global variables remain.
steps.keyInsight: a is 10 (var overwrote the global), b is 2, c is 3 (block variables are gone)
steps.misconception: It's easy to assume var a would only be 10 inside the block. In reality, the global a itself was changed!

quiz.explanation:
Declaring var x in the same scope where let x is already declared causes a SyntaxError.
Because var ignores the block, it tries to redeclare x in the global scope, which conflicts with the let declaration.

misconceptions.wrong: var is also only valid inside its block
misconceptions.correct:
var only follows **function scope**.
It ignores if/for blocks and can accidentally behave like a global variable.
misconceptions.why:
It's a relic from the early days of JavaScript design.
Because it's the main culprit of unintended global variable overwrites, modern JS avoids it.

misconceptions.wrong: let and const are the same thing
misconceptions.correct: Both are block-scoped, but const cannot be reassigned.
misconceptions.why:
const is the keyword for constants.
However, the properties of an object declared with const can still be changed.

keyTakeaway: var = function scope (ignores blocks), let/const = block scope
